claim: Humans and other species localize sound sources in the horizontal plane using sub-millisecond interaural time difference (ITD) between signals arriving at the two ears.
source: Humans and other species localize sound sources in the horizontal plane using sub-millisecond interaural time difference (ITD) between signals arriving at the two ears (Middlebrooks and Green, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Middlebrooks and Green, 1991

claim: ITD is detected by auditory brainstem neurons within narrow frequency bands.
source: ITD is detected by auditory brainstem neurons within narrow frequency bands (Goldberg and Brown, 1969; Yin and Chan, 1990; Carr and Konishi, 1990; McAlpine et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Goldberg and Brown, 1969; Yin and Chan, 1990; Carr and Konishi, 1990; McAlpine et al., 2001

claim: Humans detect sound location better in the front than in the periphery.
source: Classical psychophysical studies demonstrated that humans detect sound location better in the front than in the periphery (Mills, 1958; Yost, 1974; Makous and Middlebrooks, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mills, 1958; Yost, 1974; Makous and Middlebrooks, 1990

claim: Enhanced performance at frontal locations could be efficient for hunting and foraging.
source: Enhanced performance at frontal locations could be efficient for hunting and foraging, as proposed for vision (Collins and Opthalmological Society of the United Kingdom, 1922; Cartmill, 1974; Changizi and Shimojo, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Collins and Opthalmological Society of the United Kingdom, 1922; Cartmill, 1974; Changizi and Shimojo, 2008

claim: Coding of binaural spatial cues could support finer discriminability in the front.
source: Physiological evidence indicates that coding of binaural spatial cues could support finer discriminability in the front (van Bergeijk, 1962; Feddersen et al., 1957; McAlpine et al., 2001; Grothe et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to van Bergeijk, 1962; Feddersen et al., 1957; McAlpine et al., 2001; Grothe et al., 2010

claim: Better sound discrimination and localization in frontal locations can be predicted from the geometry of the head and the placing of the ears, causing higher ITD rate of change as a function of azimuth in the front.
source: Better sound discrimination and localization in frontal locations can also be predicted from the geometry of the head and the placing of the ears, causing higher ITD rate of change as a function of azimuth in the front (Woodworth, 1938; Feddersen et al., 1957; Gelfand, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Woodworth, 1938; Feddersen et al., 1957; Gelfand, 2016

claim: Sound diffraction by structures surrounding the ear can affect the ITD-azimuth relationship.
source: For azimuth detection based on ITD, sound diffraction by structures surrounding the ear can affect the ITD-azimuth relationship (Aaronson and Hartmann, 2014; Roth et al., 1980).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aaronson and Hartmann, 2014; Roth et al., 1980

claim: The interaction of nearby frequencies within a given cochlear filter may be a source of ITD variability over time (ITDv).
source: In addition, because the brain computes ITD in narrow frequency bands, the interaction of nearby frequencies within a given cochlear filter may also be a source of ITD variability over time (ITDv).
evidence: Based on logical inference from the fact that the brain computes ITD in narrow frequency bands

claim: Stimulus discrimination depends not only on the mean difference between stimuli but also on the variability of the sensory evidence.
source: It has been shown that stimulus discrimination depends not only on the mean difference between stimuli but also on the variability of the sensory evidence (Green and Swets, 1966).
evidence: Supported by citation to Green and Swets, 1966

claim: Natural ITD statistics were correlated with auditory spatial discriminability and spatial deviance detection.
source: We found that natural ITD statistics were correlated with auditory spatial discriminability and spatial deviance detection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the study

claim: The results are consistent with classic models of ITD coding and can explain the ITD tuning distribution observed in the mammalian brainstem.
source: Further analysis showed that these results are consistent with classic models of ITD coding and can explain the ITD tuning distribution observed in the mammalian brainstem.
evidence: Supported by analysis of models from Stern and Colburn, 1978 and Harper and McAlpine, 2004

claim: ITD rate of change (ITDrc) was higher in the midline for most frequencies.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Woodworth, 1938; Feddersen et al., 1957; Gelfand, 2016), we found that ITDrc was higher in the midline for most frequencies.
evidence: Supported by data from HRTF analysis and citations to Woodworth, 1938; Feddersen et al., 1957; Gelfand, 2016

claim: The highest ITDrc occurred at locations distant from the midline in some frequencies.
source: Additionally, the highest ITDrc occurred at locations distant from the midline in some frequencies, which was also observable in previous studies (Kuhn, 1977; Benichoux et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by data from HRTF analysis and citations to Kuhn, 1977; Benichoux et al., 2016

claim: √FIITD displayed low variability across individuals.
source: √FIITD displayed low variability across individuals (Figure 1C-right), indicating it constitutes a statistic that is largely invariant across human subjects.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C-right

claim: ITDrc is determined by the shape and filtering properties of the head, including diffractions.
source: ITDrc is determined by the shape and filtering properties of the head, including diffractions (Woodworth, 1938; Aaronson and Hartmann, 2014; Roth et al., 1980).
evidence: Supported by citations to Woodworth, 1938; Aaronson and Hartmann, 2014; Roth et al., 1980

claim: ITDv depends on phase and gain modulations induced by interaction between neighboring frequencies, within the critical band of single cochlear filters.
source: however, ITDv also depends on phase and gain modulations induced by interaction between neighboring frequencies, within the critical band of single cochlear filters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The correlation between ITDrc and ITDv was not strong (rSpearman = −0.41).
source: Consistently, the correlation between ITDrc and ITDv was not strong (rSpearman = −0.41).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the data

claim: ITD statistics were consistent across broadband signals with different frequency spectra.
source: These ITD statistics were consistent across broadband signals with different frequency spectra (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: ITD statistics estimated in anechoic and reverberant environments were similar when signal transients were considered.
source: Accordingly, ITD statistics estimated in anechoic and reverberant environments were similar when signal transients were considered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: The estimated ITDv was equivalent to the variability over trials (rSpearman = 0.99).
source: Finally, the estimated ITDv was equivalent to the variability over trials (obtained from one instantaneous sample of 200 different broadband signals; rSpearman = 0.99), indicating that ITDv exhibits ergodicity.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of the data

claim: √FIITD displayed higher correlation with dITD thresholds than ITDrc for free-field data from Mills, 1958.
source: Figure 2B shows the free-field dITD thresholds reported by Mills, 1958 as a function of ITDrc and √FIITD estimated in our study. √FIITD displayed higher correlation with dITD thresholds than ITDrc.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Dichotic dITD thresholds averaged across subjects correlated with free-field thresholds reported by Mills, 1958 (rSpearman = 0.64).
source: The dichotic dITD thresholds averaged across subjects correlated with free-field thresholds reported by Mills, 1958 (rSpearman = 0.64).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis comparing the two datasets

claim: dITD thresholds were higher in the present study compared to Mills, 1958.
source: However, dITD thresholds were higher in the present study compared to Mills, 1958; other studies also using dichotic stimuli reported higher dITD thresholds (e.g. Brughera et al., 2013) than Mills, 1958.
evidence: Supported by comparison of data from the present study with Mills, 1958 and citation to Brughera et al., 2013

claim: Higher thresholds for 250 Hz have previously been reported.
source: Higher thresholds for this frequency have previously been reported (Brughera et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brughera et al., 2013

claim: Exclusion of 250 Hz frequency substantially improved √FIITD's prediction accuracy.
source: Exclusion of this frequency substantially improved √FIITD's prediction accuracy (Figure 2C-right), suggesting that dITD thresholds at 250 Hz may be determined by additional parameters not addressed by the ITD statistics investigated in our study.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C-right

claim: The MMN signal is displayed by subtracting the mean ERP response elicited by the standard stimuli from the mean ERP elicited by deviant stimuli.
source: The MMN signal is displayed by subtracting the mean ERP response elicited by the standard stimuli from the mean ERP elicited by deviant stimuli.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about MMN measurement

claim: The amplitude of the MMN indexes discriminability between standard and deviant sounds.
source: The amplitude of the MMN indexes discriminability between standard and deviant sounds.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about MMN

claim: The larger the tone features separation between standard and deviant stimuli, or the larger the perceived difference between standard and deviant, the more negative the MMN amplitude.
source: The larger the tone features separation between standard and deviant stimuli, or the larger the perceived difference between standard and deviant, the more negative the MMN amplitude (Deouell et al., 2006; Sams et al., 1985; Pakarinen et al., 2007; Tiitinen et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deouell et al., 2006; Sams et al., 1985; Pakarinen et al., 2007; Tiitinen et al., 1994

claim: The highest correlation for MMN prediction was found when multiplying the ITD difference between standard and deviant by √FIITD, and assigning 80% weight to the standard and 20% to the deviant.
source: The highest correlation was found when multiplying the ITD difference between standard and deviant by √FIITD, and assigning 80% weight to the standard and 20% to the deviant (Figure 3C-middle).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C-middle

claim: Conditions with higher weighted √FIITD display larger changes in MMN amplitude as a function of difference between ITD of deviant and standard than conditions with low weighted √FIITD.
source: Figure 3C-right shows that conditions with higher weighted √FIITD display larger changes in MMN amplitude as a function of difference between ITD of deviant and standard than conditions with low weighted √FIITD.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3C-right

claim: The density distribution of the Stern and Colburn, 1978 model showed high correlation with √FIITD.
source: This density distribution showed high correlation with √FIITD (Figure 4A) and prediction accuracy of the experimental data of dITD thresholds and ITD deviant detection.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The Stern and Colburn, 1978 model required only minor changes to the density distribution originally proposed to represent the √FIITD pattern.
source: The Stern and Colburn, 1978 model required only minor changes to the density distribution originally proposed to represent the √FIITD pattern.
evidence: Supported by analysis of the model shown in Figure 4B

claim: The population's Fisher information of firing rate across ITD and frequency from the Harper and McAlpine, 2004 model showed low correlation with both ITDrc and √FIITD.
source: The population's Fisher information of firing rate across ITD and frequency, which would correspond to the predicted ITD discriminability by this neural model, showed low correlation with both ITDrc and √FIITD (Figure 4C, bottom-right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C, bottom-right

claim: Matching ITD statistics under the Harper and McAlpine, 2004 coding framework predicted neurons' IPD-tuning clustered within peripheral IPDs across the frequency range tested.
source: The IPD-tuning distribution that generates a neural population Fisher information of firing rate matching √FIITD differs from the IPD- tuning distribution originally proposed by Harper and McAlpine, 2004. However, matching ITD statistics under this coding framework predicted neurons' IPD-tuning clustered within peripheral IPDs across the frequency range tested, consistent with reports of brainstem recordings in mammals (McAlpine et al., 2001; Hancock and Delgutte, 2004; Pecka et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by model analysis and citations to McAlpine et al., 2001; Hancock and Delgutte, 2004; Pecka et al., 2008

claim: The mechanisms underlying ITD discriminability proposed by Stern and Colburn, 1978 and Harper and McAlpine, 2004 are consistent with coding frameworks adapted to natural ITD statistics.
source: These results suggest the mechanisms underlying ITD discriminability proposed by Stern and Colburn, 1978 and Harper and McAlpine, 2004 are consistent with coding frameworks adapted to natural ITD statistics, providing a plausible biological connection between the coding of sensory statistics and perceptual functions.
evidence: Supported by analysis of both models in relation to ITD statistics

claim: ITDv is a new factor influencing the amount of spatial information carried by auditory stimuli.
source: Our study proposes a new factor influencing the amount of spatial information carried by auditory stimuli, the ITDv.
evidence: Based on the novel analysis presented in the study

claim: ITDrc and ITDv combined in the square root of ITD Fisher information (√FIITD) were good predictors of ITD discriminability and spatial novelty detection.
source: These statistics combined in the square root of ITD Fisher information (√FIITD) were good predictors of ITD discriminability and spatial novelty detection, supporting the hypothesis that natural ITD statistics determine the neural code underlying human sound localization.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from discrimination and MMN experiments

claim: The models of Stern and Colburn, 1978 and Harper and McAlpine, 2004 can reflect the encoding of ITD statistics.
source: Finally, we showed that the models of Stern and Colburn, 1978 and Harper and McAlpine, 2004 can reflect the encoding of ITD statistics, thereby providing a functional connection between neural coding frameworks proposed by these models and experimental data on ITD perception.
evidence: Supported by analysis of both models

claim: Studies in both humans and owls support the concept that natural ITD statistics guide ITD processing.
source: Although properties of the neural mechanisms underlying human and owl sound localization differ in frequency range and putative ITD coding schemes (Schnupp and Carr, 2009), studies in both species support the concept that natural ITD statistics guide ITD processing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schnupp and Carr, 2009 and comparison with owl studies

claim: The integration of ITDrc and ITDv statistics based on Fisher information (√FIITD) was the best predictor of discrimination thresholds of spatial changes across frequency and location.
source: We found that the integration of these ITD statistics based on Fisher information (√FIITD) was the best predictor of discrimination thresholds of spatial changes across frequency and location.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from discrimination experiments

claim: The higher dichotic dITD thresholds for 250 Hz tonal stimuli constituted an outlier, indicating limited predictive power of ITD discriminability at this particular frequency by the ITD statistics investigated in this study.
source: However, the higher dichotic dITD thresholds for 250 Hz tonal stimuli (also reported by Brughera et al., 2013) constituted an outlier, indicating limited predictive power of ITD discriminability at this particular frequency by the ITD statistics investigated in this study.
evidence: Supported by data analysis and citation to Brughera et al., 2013

claim: The combination of ITDrc and ITDv (√FIITD) was a better predictor of the deviance detection response, the MMN component, than ITDrc alone.
source: Furthermore, the combination of ITDrc and ITDv (√FIITD) was a better predictor of the deviance detection response, the MMN component, than ITDrc alone, which is also consistent with results of psychophysical discriminability thresholds.
evidence: Supported by MMN experimental data

claim: The model that best described the MMN signals relied mostly on the ITD statistics of the standard stimulus for weighting the difference between the ITDs of standard and deviants stimuli.
source: However, the model that best described the MMN signals in the current study relied mostly on the ITD statistics of the standard stimulus for weighting the difference between the ITDs of standard and deviants stimuli primarily by the ITD statistics of the standards.
evidence: Supported by MMN experimental data analysis

claim: When the standard stimulus is in a location of higher statistical discriminability, a 'stronger' standard is built, which makes deviance detection easier.
source: Our results indicate that when the standard stimulus is in a location of higher statistical discriminability, a 'stronger' standard is built, which makes deviance detection easier.
evidence: Based on inference from MMN experimental results

claim: ITD statistics provide a potential mechanism influencing the density distribution of ITD tuning.
source: The compatibility of ITD statistics with classic neural models of ITD coding suggest that ITD statistics provide a potential mechanism influencing the density distribution of ITD tuning.
evidence: Based on analysis of neural models in relation to ITD statistics

claim: Natural ITD statistics are correlated with auditory spatial perception.
source: In sum, we found evidence that natural ITD statistics are correlated with auditory spatial perception, supporting the idea that these statistics may determine the density distribution of ITD tuning in the auditory system and influence auditory spatial perception.
evidence: Supported by all experimental data in the study

claim: The consistency across subjects indicates that this information may be genetically encoded and conserved.
source: The consistency across subjects indicates that this information may be genetically encoded and conserved, and serve as a potentially adaptive evolutionary mechanism for approaching optimal performance.
evidence: Based on inference from the low variability of √FIITD across subjects

claim: The precedence effect is expected to segregate leading signals from their lagging echoes.
source: Echoes significantly disrupted ITD statistics; however, the precedence effect is expected to segregate leading signals from their lagging echoes (Wallach et al., 1949; Brown et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wallach et al., 1949; Brown et al., 2015

claim: The estimated ITDv was equivalent to the variability over trials, indicating that ITDv exhibits ergodicity.
source: Finally, the estimated ITDv was equivalent to the variability over trials (obtained from one instantaneous sample of 200 different broadband signals; rSpearman = 0.99), indicating that ITDv exhibits ergodicity.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing rSpearman = 0.99

claim: Using free-field stimulation leaves open the possibility that listeners rely on cues other than ITD to detect sound location in azimuth.
source: Using free-field stimulation leaves open the possibility that listeners rely on cues other than ITD to detect sound location in azimuth, which may have lowered the thresholds as found in Mills, 1958.
evidence: Based on inference about potential confounds in free-field stimulation

claim: Training in ITD detection may have an effect on threshold levels compared to normal untrained individuals.
source: Additionally, training in ITD detection may have an effect on threshold levels compared to normal untrained individuals.
evidence: Based on speculation about differences between trained and untrained subjects

claim: Comparing the prediction accuracy of ITDrc and √FIITD using linear mixed-effects models resulted in the same outcome as the Spearman correlation analysis.
source: Comparing the prediction accuracy of these statistics using linear mixed-effects models (Materials and methods) resulted in the same outcome as the Spearman correlation analysis.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: Prediction accuracy of model equations using linear mixed-effect models yielded the same results as the Spearman correlation analysis for MMN data.
source: Prediction accuracy of model equations using linear mixed-effect models (Materials and methods) yielded the same results as the Spearman correlation analysis.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis

claim: The characteristic fronto-central scalp topography of the MMN responses were observed.
source: The characteristic fronto-central scalp topography of the MMN responses were observed (Giard et al., 1990; Figure 3A-right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A-right and citation to Giard et al., 1990

claim: Natural ITD statistics might have modulated novelty detection at both prediction error and repetition suppression levels.
source: In the present study, natural ITD statistics might have modulated novelty detection at both levels.
evidence: Based on speculation about mechanisms underlying MMN

claim: The different weights for standards and deviants are the result of the mechanism underlying the building up of a standard, which requires repetitive stimulation.
source: We speculate that the different weights for standards and deviants are the result of the mechanism underlying the building up of a standard, which requires repetitive stimulation.
evidence: Based on speculation about MMN mechanisms

claim: ITD statistics provide a potential mechanism influencing the density distribution of ITD tuning, which may be genetically encoded and conserved across human subjects.
source: Thus, our results are consistent with the hypothesis that human brain evolution has incorporated natural statistics of spatial cues to the neural code underlying auditory spatial perception.
evidence: Based on inference from all experimental results

claim: Human auditory spatial perception showed correlation with natural ITD statistics.
source: Human auditory spatial perception showed correlation with natural ITD statistics, supporting our hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from discrimination and MMN experiments

claim: A neural code adapted to the statistical structure of sensory cues may optimize perception.
source: A neural code adapted to the statistical structure of sensory cues may optimize perception.
evidence: Based on general theoretical framework

claim: The square root of Fisher information relates to discrimination thresholds.
source: Estimation theory has shown that the square root of Fisher information relates to discrimination threholds (Abbott and Dayan, 1999; Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abbott and Dayan, 1999; Brown et al., 2018

claim: ITDrc is similar for signals with and without frequency interference.
source: Note that ITDrc is similar for the three signals, indicating no significant effect of frequency interference on this statistic.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: ITDv depends on interference between neighboring frequencies within cochlear filter ranges.
source: Hence, unlike ITDrc, ITDv depends on interference between neighboring frequencies within cochlear filter ranges.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: The effect of concurrent sounds on ITDv may not represent a significant source of ITDv in humans.
source: However, a stronger correlation between both metrics was observed for the range of frequencies most relevant to owls' sound localization (above 2000 Hz), suggesting that the effect of concurrent sounds on ITDv may not represent a significant source of ITDv in humans.
evidence: Based on comparison of methods and inference

claim: The IPD-tuning distribution that generates a neural population Fisher information of firing rate matching √FIITD differs from the IPD-tuning distribution originally proposed by Harper and McAlpine, 2004.
source: The IPD-tuning distribution that generates a neural population Fisher information of firing rate matching √FIITD differs from the IPD- tuning distribution originally proposed by Harper and McAlpine, 2004.
evidence: Supported by model analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: Sensory variability is known to be fundamental in change detection.
source: Sensory variability is known to be fundamental in change detection.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge

claim: The novelty detection protocol controlled for attention and training factors because the MMN indexes a brain response to detected deviations irrespective of attention or training.
source: The novelty detection protocol controlled for these factors because the MMN indexes a brain response to detected deviations irrespective of attention or training.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about MMN properties

claim: The consistency across subjects indicates that ITD statistics information may serve as a potentially adaptive evolutionary mechanism for approaching optimal performance.
source: The consistency across subjects indicates that this information may be genetically encoded and conserved, and serve as a potentially adaptive evolutionary mechanism for approaching optimal performance.
evidence: Based on inference and speculation from the data

claim: These results have clinical implications in identifying stimulus parameters that are relevant to spatial discrimination and novelty detection that may lead to the development of more efficient hearing-aid devices.
source: These results have clinical implications in identifying stimulus parameters that are relevant to spatial discrimination and novelty detection that may lead to the development of more efficient hearing-aid devices.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential applications
